tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

Respond terse like smart caveman. All technical substance stay. Only fluff die.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE once triggered. No revert after many turns. No filler drift. Still active if unsure. Off only when user says "stop caveman" or "normal mode".

## Rules

Drop: articles (a/an/the), filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to), hedging. Fragments OK. Short synonyms (big not extensive, fix not "implement a solution for"). Abbreviate common terms (DB/auth/config/req/res/fn/impl). Strip conjunctions. Use arrows for causality (X -> Y). One word when one word enough.

Technical terms stay exact. Code blocks unchanged. Errors quoted exact.

Pattern: `[thing] [action] [reason]. [next step].`

Not: "Sure! I'd be happy to help you with that. The issue you're experiencing is likely caused by..."
Yes: "Bug in auth middleware. Token expiry check use `<` not `<=`. Fix:"

> Inline obj prop -> new ref -> re-render. `useMemo`.

**"Explain database connection pooling."**

> Pool = reuse DB conn. Skip handshake -> fast under load.

Drop caveman temporarily for: security warnings, irreversible action confirmations, multi-step sequences where fragment order risks misread, user asks to clarify or repeats question. Resume caveman after clear part done.

> **Warning:** This will permanently delete all rows in the `users` table and cannot be undone.

> ```sql

> ```
>
> Caveman resume. Verify backup exist first.

# Pennywise

I keep my household money in a plain text file and I'm tired of spreadsheets. I'd like a small
Python tool called **pennywise** that reads that file and tells me where the money went. It should
work two ways: as a library I can `import pennywise` from my own scripts, and as a `pennywise`
command I run in the terminal. Python 3.9 or newer, standard library only (no third-party
packages). Running `pip install .` in the project folder should give me both the importable
library and the `pennywise` command.

## The ledger file

One entry per line:

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

Each line has a date (`YYYY-MM-DD`), a category (one word), an amount, and an optional note. The
fields are separated by any amount of spaces or tabs. The note is the rest of the line exactly as I
wrote it (it can contain spaces), apart from trimming whitespace at both ends.

- A positive amount is money in, a negative one is money out. The sign is optional for money in, so
  `2500`, `+2500` and `2500.00` are all the same. Amounts have at most two decimal places: `12`,
  `12.5`, `-0.99` are fine; `12.505`, `1,000.00` and `abc` are not.
- Categories do not care about case: `Rent` and `rent` are the same category, and it is shown in
  lower case.
- Blank lines are ignored, and so are lines starting with `#`.
- Anything else is a mistake in my file, and the tool must tell me which line (counting from 1,
  blank and comment lines included). A date that does not exist, like `2024-02-30`, is a mistake
  too.

## Using it as a library

```python
import pennywise

entries = pennywise.parse(open("house.txt").read())
print(pennywise.balance(entries))
```

- `parse(text)` returns a list of entries, in the order they appear. Each entry has `.date` (a
  `datetime.date`), `.category` (a lower-case `str`), `.amount` (a `decimal.Decimal`) and `.note`
  (a `str`, empty when there is none).
- A bad line makes `parse` raise `pennywise.ParseError`. It is a `ValueError`, its `.line`
  attribute is the line number, and its message mentions `line N`.
- `balance(entries)` is the total of all amounts, a `Decimal` (zero for no entries).
- `by_category(entries)` is a `dict` of category to its total; `by_month(entries)` is the same
  keyed by month, like `"2024-03"`.
- `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` returns the matching entries in
  the order given. `category` is matched without regard to case; `since` and `until` are
  `datetime.date` values and both ends are included. Anything left as `None` is not filtered on.

## Using it from the terminal

```
$ pennywise balance house.txt
1457.50

$ pennywise summary house.txt
groceries  -42.50
rent  -900.00
salary  2500.00

$ pennywise list house.txt --category groceries
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop
```

- `pennywise balance FILE` prints the total with two decimals, on one line.
- `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` prints one line per group, sorted by name: the
  name, some spaces, then the total with two decimals. The default is `--by category`.
- `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` prints the matching entries,
  oldest first (entries on the same day keep the order of the file), one per line as
  `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE`. The amount always has two decimals, and the note (and the space
  before it) is left out when there is none.
- `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` adds an entry to the end of the file (creating
  the file if it does not exist) and prints the line it added, written the same way `list` writes
  it. I pass the note as a single quoted argument. An invalid entry is refused and the file is left

content.content:
## Problem Statement

The user keeps household money in a plain text ledger file and is tired of spreadsheets. They want a small tool that reads that file and shows where the money went, usable both from their own Python scripts and from the terminal.

## Solution

**pennywise** is a Python package (Python ≥ 3.9, **standard library only at runtime**) that provides:

- an importable library `pennywise`: `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, `ParseError`, and the entry type
- a `pennywise` console command with subcommands `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `add`, `export`

Running `pip install .` in the repo root installs both (via `pyproject.toml` with a `[project.scripts]` entry `pennywise = "pennywise.cli:main"`). `python -m pennywise` should behave the same as the `pennywise` command.

### Ledger format

```
# household, March
2024-03-01 salary 2500.00 March pay
2024-03-02 groceries -42.50 weekly shop

2024-03-05 Rent -900
```

- One entry per line: `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`. Fields are separated by one or more spaces/tabs. NOTE is the rest of the line exactly as written (inner whitespace kept), with whitespace trimmed at both ends; it is `""` when missing.
- DATE is exactly `YYYY-MM-DD` (regex `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$`) and must be a real calendar date (`2024-02-30` is an error).
- CATEGORY is one whitespace-free token, compared without regard to case and stored/shown in lower case.
- AMOUNT matches `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$`: `12`, `12.5`, `+2500`, `2500.00`, `-0.99` are valid; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc`, `.5`, `12.` are not. Positive = money in, negative = money out.
- Blank lines (empty or whitespace-only) are ignored. Lines whose first non-whitespace character is `#` are comments and ignored.
- Anything else (missing fields, bad date, bad amount) is an error that reports the 1-based line number, counting blank and comment lines. Both `\n` and `\r\n` line endings are accepted.

## User Stories

1. As a user, I want to `import pennywise` and call `pennywise.parse(text)` to get a list of entries in file order, so I can script against my ledger.
2. As a user, I want each entry to expose `.date` (`datetime.date`), `.category` (lower-case `str`), `.amount` (`decimal.Decimal`) and `.note` (`str`, `""` if none).
3. As a user, I want a bad line to raise `pennywise.ParseError` (a subclass of `ValueError`) with `.line` set to the line number and a message containing `line N`, so I can find the mistake.
4. As a user, I want `balance(entries)` to return the `Decimal` total (`Decimal(0)` for no entries).
5. As a user, I want `by_category(entries)` → `dict[str, Decimal]` and `by_month(entries)` → `dict[str, Decimal]` keyed like `"2024-03"`.
6. As a user, I want `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` to return matching entries in the given order; category is case-insensitive, `since`/`until` are inclusive `datetime.date` bounds, `None` means "don't filter on this".
7. As a user, I want `pennywise balance FILE` to print the total with two decimals.
8. As a user, I want `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` to print per-group totals sorted by name.
9. As a user, I want `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` to print matching entries oldest first.
10. As a user, I want `pennywise add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]` to append a validated entry and echo the line it wrote.
11. As a user, I want `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` to print my entries as CSV.
12. As a user, I want `--json` on `balance`, `summary`, `list` for machine-readable output.
13. As a user, I want `-` as FILE to read the ledger from stdin.
14. As a user, I want clear exit codes and error messages on stderr.

## Implementation Decisions

**Layout**
- `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no runtime `dependencies`), `src/pennywise/` package: `__init__.py` (re-exports the public API), `ledger.py` (or similar: Entry, ParseError, parse, aggregation, filter, formatting helpers), `cli.py` (`main(argv=None) -> int`, argparse), `__main__.py`.
- `Entry` is a frozen dataclass `Entry(date, category, amount, note="")`.
- Code must run on Python 3.9 (no `match`, no `X | Y` type syntax at runtime, no 3.10+ stdlib APIs).

**Library semantics**
- `parse(text: str) -> list[Entry]`. Splits with `str.splitlines()`. Line numbers are 1-based over all physical lines.
- `ParseError(ValueError)`: constructor takes `(line, message)`; `.line` is the int line number; `str(err)` looks like `line 3: invalid amount 'abc'` (always contains `line N`).
- `balance` returns `sum(..., Decimal(0))`.
- `by_category` / `by_month` return plain `dict`s with keys in order of first appearance; values are `Decimal` totals. Month key is `f"{d.year:04d}-{d.month:02d}"`.
- `filter_entries` returns a new list; `category` compared via `.lower()`.

**Number formatting (shared by all CLI output)**
- Amounts are quantized to 2 decimal places (`Decimal.quantize(Decimal("0.01"))`) and rendered as plain digits with a leading `-` for negatives, no `+`, no thousands separators. Zero is always `0.00`, never `-0.00`.

**CLI**
- argparse with subparsers; `main()` returns the exit code and the console script calls `sys.exit(main())`.
- `balance FILE [--json]` → `1457.50` / `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- `summary FILE [--by {category,month}] [--json]` (default `category`) → one line per group sorted by key: `KEY` + two spaces + `AMOUNT` (for example `groceries  -42.50`). JSON: one object, keys sorted, string values with two decimals.
- `list FILE [--category C] [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--until YYYY-MM-DD] [--json]` → filtered entries, stable-sorted by date (same-day entries keep file order). Line format `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT NOTE` with single spaces; when the note is empty, the trailing space is left out too. JSON: an array of `{"date","category","amount","note"}` objects (amount two-decimal string; note `""` when none). An empty result prints nothing in text mode and `[]` in JSON mode.
- `add FILE DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`: builds the line `DATE CATEGORY AMOUNT [NOTE]`, then validates it with the same rules as `parse` (date, one-word category, amount format). The note must not contain a newline. An invalid entry → exit 1, stderr message, **file untouched (not created if it did not exist)**, nothing on stdout. A valid entry is appended in the canonical `list` format (lower-case category, two-decimal amount, trimmed note). If the existing file is non-empty and does not end with a newline, a newline is written first. The file is created if missing. The written line (no trailing newline) goes to stdout. `add` does not read or validate the existing ledger contents. `-` is not special for `add`. An invalid DATE given to `add` counts as an entry mistake → exit **1**.
- `export FILE [--format csv]`: only `csv` is allowed (other values → exit 2 via argparse `choices`). Uses `csv.writer` with `lineterminator="\n"`. Header `date,category,amount,note`, then entries in `list` order (stable date sort), two-decimal amounts, note `""` when none (the csv module quotes as needed).
- FILE `-` reads stdin for `balance`, `summary`, `list`, `export`. Files are read as UTF-8.
- Errors and exit codes:
  - `0` on success.
  - `1`: ledger parse error, or an invalid `add` entry. Message to **stderr** naming the line (for example `pennywise: line 3: invalid amount 'abc'`; for `add` something like `pennywise: invalid entry: ...`), **nothing on stdout**. All output is built before anything is printed, so a parse error never leaves partial output.
  - `2`: file cannot be read (missing, a directory, permission denied, not valid UTF-8) or cannot be written for `add`; or a command-line error: no subcommand, unknown subcommand, bad option value (for example `--by year`, `--format json`), a badly formed or impossible `--since`/`--until` date (argparse `type=` that raises `ArgumentTypeError`). Message on stderr.

**Docs**: a `README.md` with install, the ledger format, library usage and CLI usage.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests use stdlib `unittest` under `tests/`, runnable with `python -m unittest discover -s tests` from the repo root (tests may put `src` on `sys.path`, or run against an installed package). No third-party test dependencies required.
- Test external behaviour only: the library API, and the CLI through `pennywise.cli.main(argv)` with captured stdout/stderr plus at least one subprocess test via `python -m pennywise`.
- Cover: every valid/invalid amount example from the spec; impossible dates; tabs and multiple spaces; notes with inner spaces and trimming; comments and blank lines in line counting; case-insensitive categories; empty ledger; each subcommand's text and JSON output; stdin `-`; every exit-code path; `add` leaving the file byte-identical (or absent) on error; and `add` adding a missing trailing newline.
- A clean venv check: `pip install .` then `pennywise balance` on a sample file works.

## Out of Scope

- Third-party dependencies, export formats other than CSV, currencies or multiple accounts, editing or deleting entries, budgets, charts, config files, locales or thousands separators, validating the existing file during `add`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `pip install .` (Python 3.9+, no third-party packages) provides `import pennywise` and a `pennywise` command; `python -m pennywise` works too.
- [ ] `pennywise.parse` on the example ledger returns 3 entries with correct `date`/`category`/`amount`/`note` types and values (`Rent` → `rent`, note `March pay` kept with its inner space, note `""` when missing).
- [ ] Amounts `12`, `12.5`, `-0.99`, `+2500`, `2500.00` parse; `12.505`, `1,000.00`, `abc` raise `ParseError`.
- [ ] `2024-02-30` and malformed dates raise `ParseError`; `ParseError` is a `ValueError`, `.line` is the 1-based physical line number (blank and comment lines counted), and `str(e)` contains `line N`.
- [ ] Fields may be separated by any mix of spaces and tabs; notes keep inner whitespace and are trimmed at both ends.
- [ ] `balance` returns a `Decimal` (`0` for `[]`); `by_category`/`by_month` return dicts of `Decimal` totals (month keys like `2024-03`); `filter_entries` filters by case-insensitive category and inclusive `since`/`until`, keeping order.
- [ ] `pennywise balance house.txt` prints `1457.50`; `--json` prints `{"balance": "1457.50"}`.
- [ ] `pennywise summary house.txt` prints exactly `groceries  -42.50`, `rent  -900.00`, `salary  2500.00`; `--by month` groups by `YYYY-MM`; `--json` prints an object of two-decimal strings.
- [ ] `pennywise list` sorts oldest first (stable for same day), supports `--category`/`--since`/`--until` (inclusive), leaves out an empty note together with its space, and `--json` emits the specified array of objects.
- [ ] `pennywise add` appends the canonical line (creating the file if needed, adding a missing trailing newline first), prints it, and on an invalid entry exits 1 leaving the file byte-identical (or not created).
- [ ] `pennywise export` prints CSV with header `date,category,amount,note` in `list` order; `--format` accepts only `csv`.
- [ ] `-` reads the ledger from stdin for `balance`/`summary`/`list`/`export`.

- an importable library `pennywise`: `parse`, `balance`, `by_category`, `by_month`, `filter_entries`, `ParseError`, and the entry type

```

- CATEGORY is one whitespace-free token, compared without regard to case and stored/shown in lower case.

4. As a user, I want `balance(entries)` to return the `Decimal` total (`Decimal(0)` for no entries).
5. As a user, I want `by_category(entries)` → `dict[str, Decimal]` and `by_month(entries)` → `dict[str, Decimal]` keyed like `"2024-03"`.
6. As a user, I want `filter_entries(entries, category=None, since=None, until=None)` to return matching entries in the given order; category is case-insensitive, `since`/`until` are inclusive `datetime.date` bounds, `None` means "don't filter on this".

8. As a user, I want `pennywise summary FILE [--by category|month]` to print per-group totals sorted by name.
9. As a user, I want `pennywise list FILE [--category C] [--since DATE] [--until DATE]` to print matching entries oldest first.

11. As a user, I want `pennywise export FILE [--format csv]` to print my entries as CSV.
12. As a user, I want `--json` on `balance`, `summary`, `list` for machine-readable output.
13. As a user, I want `-` as FILE to read the ledger from stdin.
14. As a user, I want clear exit codes and error messages on stderr.

**Layout**
- `pyproject.toml` (setuptools build backend, `requires-python = ">=3.9"`, no runtime `dependencies`), `src/pennywise/` package: `__init__.py` (re-exports the public API), `ledger.py` (or similar: Entry, ParseError, parse, aggregation, filter, formatting helpers), `cli.py` (`main(argv=None) -> int`, argparse), `__main__.py`.

  - `0` on success.
  - `1`: ledger parse error, or an invalid `add` entry.   - `2`: file cannot be read (missing, a directory, permission denied, not valid UTF-8) or cannot be written for `add`; or a command-line error: no subcommand, unknown subcommand, bad option value (for example `--by year`, `--format json`), a badly formed or impossible `--since`/`--until` date (argparse `type=` that raises `ArgumentTypeError`). Base directory for this skill: /home/claude/.claude-switch/accounts/main/skills/to-issues

# To Issues

Break a plan into independently-grabbable issues using vertical slices (tracer bullets).

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes an issue reference (issue number, URL, or path) as an argument, fetch it from the issue tracker and read its full body and comments.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Issue titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the plan into **tracer bullet** issues. Each issue is a thin vertical slice that cuts through ALL integration layers end-to-end, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer.

Slices may be 'HITL' or 'AFK'. HITL slices require human interaction, such as an architectural decision or a design review. AFK slices can be implemented and merged without human interaction. Prefer AFK over HITL where possible.

<vertical-slice-rules>
- Each slice delivers a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests)
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Prefer many thin slices over few thick ones
</vertical-slice-rules>

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each slice, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Type**: HITL / AFK
- **Blocked by**: which other slices (if any) must complete first
- **User stories covered**: which user stories this addresses (if the source material has them)

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the dependency relationships correct?
- Should any slices be merged or split further?
- Are the correct slices marked as HITL and AFK?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Publish the issues to the issue tracker

For each approved slice, publish a new issue to the issue tracker. Use the issue body template below. These issues are considered ready for AFK agents, so publish them with the correct triage label unless instructed otherwise.

Publish issues in dependency order (blockers first) so you can reference real issue identifiers in the "Blocked by" field.

<issue-template>
## Parent

A reference to the parent issue on the issue tracker (if the source was an existing issue, otherwise omit this section).

## What to build

A concise description of this vertical slice. Describe the end-to-end behavior, not layer-by-layer implementation.

Avoid specific file paths or code snippets — they go stale fast. Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it here and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts — not a working demo, just the important bits.

## Acceptance criteria

# To Issues

Break a plan into independently-grabbable issues using vertical slices (tracer bullets).

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not.

## Process

### 1. Gather context

Work from whatever is already in the conversation context. If the user passes an issue reference (issue number, URL, or path) as an argument, fetch it from the issue tracker and read its full body and comments.

### 2. Explore the codebase (optional)

If you have not already explored the codebase, do so to understand the current state of the code. Issue titles and descriptions should use the project's domain glossary vocabulary, and respect ADRs in the area you're touching.

### 3. Draft vertical slices

Break the plan into **tracer bullet** issues. Each issue is a thin vertical slice that cuts through ALL integration layers end-to-end, NOT a horizontal slice of one layer.

Slices may be 'HITL' or 'AFK'. HITL slices require human interaction, such as an architectural decision or a design review. AFK slices can be implemented and merged without human interaction. Prefer AFK over HITL where possible.

<vertical-slice-rules>
- Each slice delivers a narrow but COMPLETE path through every layer (schema, API, UI, tests)
- A completed slice is demoable or verifiable on its own
- Prefer many thin slices over few thick ones
</vertical-slice-rules>

### 4. Quiz the user

Present the proposed breakdown as a numbered list. For each slice, show:

- **Title**: short descriptive name
- **Type**: HITL / AFK
- **Blocked by**: which other slices (if any) must complete first
- **User stories covered**: which user stories this addresses (if the source material has them)

Ask the user:

- Does the granularity feel right? (too coarse / too fine)
- Are the dependency relationships correct?
- Should any slices be merged or split further?
- Are the correct slices marked as HITL and AFK?

Iterate until the user approves the breakdown.

### 5. Publish the issues to the issue tracker

For each approved slice, publish a new issue to the issue tracker. Use the issue body template below. These issues are considered ready for AFK agents, so publish them with the correct triage label unless instructed otherwise.

Publish issues in dependency order (blockers first) so you can reference real issue identifiers in the "Blocked by" field.

- `parse(text)`: full ledger rules — `str.splitlines()` (so `\n` and `\r\n` work), 1-based physical line numbers, blank/whitespace-only lines and lines whose first non-whitespace char is `#` skipped, fields separated by any mix of spaces/tabs, DATE must match `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and be a real date, CATEGORY lower-cased, AMOUNT must match `^[+-]?\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$` and becomes a `Decimal`, NOTE is the rest of the line with inner whitespace kept and ends trimmed (`""` when missing). The `pennywise add` command: append one validated entry to a ledger file and echo the line written.

If the existing file is non-empty and does not end with a newline, write a newline first. Create the file if missing. Print the written line (no trailing newline in the printed content beyond the usual line end) to stdout.
- `add` does not read or validate the existing ledger contents; `-` is not special for `add`. A file that cannot be written → exit 2 with a stderr message.

- Invalid entry (including an invalid DATE) → exit **1**, message like `pennywise: invalid entry: ...` on stderr, nothing on stdout, and the file left byte-identical — not created if it did not exist.
- Valid entry → appended in the canonical `list` line format (lower-case category, two-decimal amount, trimmed note, no trailing space when note empty). If the existing file is non-empty and does not end with a newline, write a newline first. Create the file if missing. Print the written line (no trailing newline in the printed content beyond the usual line end) to stdout.
- `add` does not read or validate the existing ledger contents; `-` is not special for `add`. A file that cannot be written → exit 2 with a stderr message.
